title: Copy a link, crown a giant
hook: New pages copy each other's links. Does the top page get a bit bigger, or far bigger?

knows: rich-get-richer: early popularity attracts more popularity (same-songs-different-hits)
doesNotKnow: how strongly the share of copying controls the size of the biggest winner

misconception: Copying other people's links changes the biggest page a little, perhaps doubling it.
objective: The learner can explain that copying a random page's link lands on a page with chance proportional to the links it already has, so raising copying from 0% to 90% turns a biggest page of about a dozen links into one with thousands, out of 10,000.

claims.text: In the stage's model, each of 10,000 new pages adds one link to an earlier page: with the copying share it picks a random earlier page and links to whatever that page links to, otherwise it links to a random earlier page.
claims.source: Lesson rule (Demo.tsx simulate). Page 0 starts the world; page i copies from pages 1..i-1 (pages that have a link) or links uniformly to pages 0..i-1. The copying model follows the brief (E&K ch. 18).

claims.text: In the stage's model of 10,000 pages, the biggest page ends with 12 to 18 links with no copying, 158 to 179 with 50% copying and 4,537 to 6,278 with 90% copying (seeds 1 to 3); per seed: 12/160/6,278, 18/179/4,537, 12/158/5,122.
claims.source: Builder's node run of the lesson's own generator (Demo.tsx simulate: mulberry32(seed), two draws per page, the same draws for every copying share), 2026-10-14. Seeds 1-3 are the first three integers, not chosen to show the result. The brief's cm re-run gave 12/18/12 and 6277/4536/5121 (one off at 90%, likely a different start rule); the brief range 4,500-6,300 holds.

claims.text: In the same runs, the top 1% of pages hold about 7% of all links with no copying, 26 to 27% at 50% and 84 to 86% at 90%.
claims.source: Builder's node run, seeds 1-3: top 100 of 10,001 pages hold 7.3/7.4/7.6% (c=0), 26.7/26.9/25.6% (c=0.5), 84.3/85.5/85.1% (c=0.9) of the 10,000 links. Readout on stage uses the top floor((i+1)/100) pages after i pages.

claims.text: A copier lands on a page with chance proportional to the links that page already has, so a page with 500 links is 500 times more likely to be copied than a page with one.
claims.source: Copying picks one of the i-1 existing links uniformly and follows it; page j is the target of deg(j) of them, so P(copy lands on j) = c * deg(j)/(i-1). E&K ch. 18 describes the same rich-get-richer equivalence.

claims.text: Without copying, every earlier page has the same chance of getting the new link.
claims.source: Lesson rule: with c = 0 the target is uniform on pages 0..i-1.

recall.question: In a copying model, new pages copy an existing link 90% of the time instead of 0%. What happens to the most-linked page?
options: It gets roughly twice as many links
It gets hundreds of times more links
recall.why: Copying a random link lands on a page in proportion to the links it already has, so the leader keeps pulling ahead: from about a dozen links to thousands out of 10,000.
